title: Enhancement: add Mollie as a payment provider option in the builder (next to Polar.sh)
body:
## Summary

Add [Mollie](https://www.mollie.com/) as a selectable payment provider in the stack builder ([better-t-stack.dev/new](https://www.better-t-stack.dev/new)), alongside the existing [Polar.sh](https://polar.sh) option.

## Motivation

The builder currently offers Polar.sh as a payments choice. Mollie is a widely-used, European-headquartered payment service provider with strong EU coverage and a broad set of local payment methods (iDEAL, Bancontact, SEPA, credit cards, Apple Pay, and more). Offering it next to Polar.sh would give teams - especially those building for European markets or with EU data-residency requirements - a first-class, batteries-included alternative without hand-rolling the integration.

## Proposal

- Add a `mollie` option to the payments selector in the web builder, positioned next to `polar.sh`.
- Scaffold the equivalent integration wiring the project already provides for Polar (SDK dependency, environment variables, and a minimal example/handler) so a generated project works out of the box.
- Mollie ships an official Node SDK (`@mollie/api-client`) and documented webhooks, so the integration shape should mirror the existing Polar provider closely.

## Alternatives

Users can integrate Mollie manually today, but a built-in option keeps parity with the existing Polar.sh experience and lowers setup friction.

Happy to help and/or open a PR if this is something the maintainers would welcome. Thanks for the great tool!

title: [CRITICAL][Smart Contract] verify_vulnerability allows double-payout and never checks/deducts the bounty pool
body:
## Summary
verify_vulnerability() does not check whether the report was already verified, does not check the BOUNTY_POOL has sufficient funds, and does not deduct the bounty from any pool. A verifier can call it repeatedly on the same report_id to re-award the bounty and repeatedly inflate the reporter's reputation/earnings.

## Severity
Critical

## Location
contracts/scanner/src/lib.rs - verify_vulnerability()

## Impact
- Double/multi-payout: repeated calls re-run update_reputation(reporter, 1, bounty_amount) and reset report.bounty_amount, so a single report can be paid many times.
- No funds check means a verifier can authorize payouts exceeding the pool (or any payout at all, since pools are fictional - see related custody issue).

## Root Cause
Missing status guard (report.status == "pending") and missing pool balance check/deduction.

## Recommended Fix
- Reject if report.status != "pending" (one-time verification).
- Check bounty_amount <= BOUNTY_POOL and subtract it from the pool atomically.
- Use the report's stored status as a state machine (pending -> verified/rejected).

## Bounty Note
Direct loss-of-funds via double-payout is a classic, high-reward finding.

title: [Feature]: verification gated release policy for auth-capture (a pact-escrow profile)
body:
### Problem or use case

auth-capture deliberately defines the hold and stays silent on the release: capture or void is a discretionary act of the captureAuthorizer. That's the right layering, but it leaves the two parties with no protocol-level way to (1) agree upfront what satisfactory delivery means for this payment, (2) verify delivery against that agreement, and (3) dispute a wrong release decision. Today the client trusts the captureAuthorizer's judgment, off-protocol.

That blocks the use case several open issues are circling: agent-to-agent task delegation where payment releases on verified completion (#1247), dispute handling when verification is contested (#2001), a correctness and dispute layer for what settlement can't see (#2887), and canonical delivery proof at settlement (#1195, #2833).

Concrete example: an agent pays $195 for a data cleaning job under auth-capture with autoCapture:false. What decides capture vs void? Today, nothing the counterparties agreed to in a machine checkable form. The acceptance tests passing or failing should be that decision, and both sides should have committed to those tests before work started.

### Proposed solution

A release-policy profile over auth-capture. No changes to the scheme itself, the profile specifies what a conformant captureAuthorizer executes:

  1. Before authorization, buyer and seller co-sign a Verifiable Task Contract: a JSON object fixing task scope by hash, price, verification method, challenge window, and the seller's bond. Canonicalized with JCS (RFC 8785), signed with JWS (RFC 7515).

  2. Release becomes mechanical. Verification passes: capture. Verification fails: void. On the optimistic path, capture fires at challenge-window expiry unless a fraud proof lands; the bond funds slashing, challenger cost reimbursement, and a capped bounty, because slashing alone doesn't fix the verifier's dilemma. Verification is graded per contract: deterministic re-execution, TEE attestation (EAT/RATS), zkML, or staked arbitration.

  3. At settlement, both parties co-sign a Work Attestation carrying the contract hash and outcome: a delivery receipt in the sense #1195 and #2833 are after, except only emittable through a bonded, escrowed contract, which is what makes accumulated receipts expensive to fake.
 
The full lifecycle is specified as an IETF Internet-Draft, draft-laxsharma-pact-00 (individual submission, Experimental). One honesty note: Section 8 of the -00 currently expresses the x402 binding as a standalone pact-escrow scheme, written against the escrow and deferred lineage that was closed in May (#873, #426). Reshaping that binding into a profile over the merged auth-capture machinery is exactly the change I'd make in -01, and this issue is me proposing it here first. Schemas and worked examples whose hashes verify in CI: https://github.com/pact-spec/spec . Draft: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-laxsharma-pact/

Concrete ask: (a) is this better shaped as a profile doc under specs/schemes/auth-capture/ or an extension under specs/extensions/? (b) If maintainers see a path, I'll draft that spec doc as a PR. It's a -00, published to be demolished; sharp edges welcome.

title: [CRITICAL][Smart Contract] Multi-sig can be bypassed: proposer controls required_approvals and execution_delay
body:
## Summary
propose_high_bounty_verification() forwards caller-supplied required_approvals and execution_delay directly into create_multi_sig_proposal() without enforcing any minimum. A single Verifier can set required_approvals=1 and execution_delay=0, then propose, approve and execute a multi-million bounty payout alone.

## Severity
Critical

## Location
contracts/scanner/src/lib.rs - propose_high_bounty_verification() and create_multi_sig_proposal()

## Impact
- The multi-signature control intended to protect high-value bounty payouts (verify_vulnerability returns MultiSigRequired for amounts > 1,000,000) is trivially bypassed.
- A single compromised/rogue Verifier can authorize arbitrary bounty_amount payouts without any second signer or timelock.

## Root Cause
propose_high_bounty_verification passes required_approvals and execution_delay verbatim. Contrast with propose_emergency_verification and propose_role_grant, which enforce minimums (>=3 approvals, >=1h; >=2 approvals, >=24h).

## Recommended Fix
- Enforce minimums server-side in propose_high_bounty_verification (e.g. required_approvals >= 2, execution_delay >= 3600).
- Also reject required_approvals == 0 and validate that required_approvals does not exceed the number of registered verifiers.

## Bounty Note
Bypass of a security control that guards treasury payouts is a direct loss-of-funds vector and highly rewarded.

It's not a problem specific this this one file - I haven't gotten any STL to import and compile from any source so far on this project. I'm running OpenSCAD 2014.03 on Mac OS X 10.9.2, and see the same thing on Linux, and on Windows.

I've run out of ideas. But I'd welcome any suggestions or help on this one. It's a noble project  (IMO) and I'm hoping someone with a fresh pair of eyes can come up with something.

title: [High] Design and publish a bug-bounty program scoped to `SECURITY.md`'s Assets-at-Risk table
body:
**Description:** `SECURITY.md` currently defers all vulnerability reporting to the org-level `SECURITY.md` for "responsible-disclosure process" instructions, but this repository has no bounty program, reward structure, or in-scope/out-of-scope definition of its own. Design and publish one, directly mapped to the specific assets and trust assumptions this repo's own `SECURITY.md` already documents (solver bonds, user swap output, protocol fees, admin privileges).

**Problem Statement & Context:** `SECURITY.md`'s Threat Model section is unusually thorough for a project at this stage — it already enumerates exactly which assets are at risk, their approximate value ("≥ 50 USDC per solver," "Unbounded" for user swap output), and five distinct named trust assumptions with their implications. That existing rigor is exactly what a well-scoped bounty program needs as its foundation, but nothing currently turns that threat model into actual reward incentives for external security researchers — a real gap ahead of the mainnet deployment `docs/mainnet-deployment-runbook.md` and `docs/pre-deploy-security-checklist.md` are both preparing for.

**Scope & Acceptance Criteria:**

- A `docs/bug-bounty-program.md` (or a dedicated section appended to `SECURITY.md`) defining severity tiers mapped explicitly to `SECURITY.md`'s existing Assets at Risk table (e.g., a finding that could drain solver bonds or user swap output is Critical; a finding limited to griefing/admin-key-blast-radius per the existing "What a compromised admin key can and cannot do" table is a lower tier), in-scope contracts/versions, and out-of-scope categories (e.g., issues already tracked in this very issue list, per the existing "Known Limitations" section).
- A clear reward structure or reward-determination process (even if final dollar amounts depend on a not-yet-established treasury per issue #37 — the program can specify tiers and a commitment to fund them once treasury infrastructure exists, rather than blocking entirely on that dependency).
- Out of scope: standing up an actual bounty-hosting platform (Immunefi, HackenProof, etc.) integration — this issue delivers the program's scope/reward-tier design as a document; platform integration is a follow-up business decision.

**Implementation Guidelines:**

1. Key files: `SECURITY.md` (Assets at Risk table, Trust Assumptions §1–5, Known Limitations — the exact source material this program's scope and severity tiers must be grounded in, not invented independently), `docs/pre-deploy-security-checklist.md` (mainnet-readiness context this program should align its urgency/timeline with).
2. Cross-reference severity tiers against concrete example findings from this very issue list (e.g., issue #82's `compute_intent_id` collision audit, issue #84's overflow audit) as worked examples of what would qualify at each tier, grounding the abstract severity definitions in real, already-identified risk categories.
3. Edge cases: explicitly address how a finding overlapping with an already-open issue in this list is handled (e.g., does filing a PR against an existing security issue qualify for a bounty, or only genuinely novel findings?) — this is a real ambiguity a Drips Wave-style contributor pool will hit immediately.
4. Testing: not applicable in the traditional sense — validate via review from someone with prior bug-bounty-program design experience, and by dry-running the severity-tier rubric against two or three real findings from this issue list's existing Security & Auditing issues.

**Definition of Done:**

- `docs/bug-bounty-program.md` written, cross-referenced from `SECURITY.md`.
- Acceptance criteria met.
- PR reviewed and approved.
- Reviewed and approved.

**Resources:** `SECURITY.md`, `docs/pre-deploy-security-checklist.md`

**Complexity:** High (200 points)

title: 🔐 Security Bounty Program — MyZubster
body:
# MyZubster Security Bounty Program

## Obiettivo
Invitare security researchers a individuare e segnalare vulnerabilità reali in MyZubster in modo responsabile, con ricompense proporzionate all'impatto e alla qualità del report.

## Scope
- MyZubster application e API pubblicamente esposte
- Autenticazione, autorizzazione e session management
- IDOR/BOLA, privilege escalation e access-control bypass
- Injection, SSRF, XSS, CSRF e vulnerabilità di business logic
- Leakage di dati sensibili
- Vulnerabilità nella supply chain o integrazioni che impattano direttamente MyZubster
- Integrazione Metasploit: solo validazione su asset esplicitamente autorizzati e senza impatto distruttivo

## Fuori scope
- DoS/DDoS o stress test distruttivi
- Social engineering, phishing o attacchi fisici
- Spam
- Vulnerabilità esclusivamente teoriche senza security impact dimostrabile
- Scansioni aggressive contro infrastrutture di terzi
- Exploit o payload contro sistemi non appartenenti a MyZubster o senza autorizzazione
- Accesso, modifica o cancellazione di dati di altri utenti oltre il minimo necessario a dimostrare l'impatto

## Fasce indicative di bounty
| Severità | Esempi | Bounty indicativa |
|---|---|---:|
| Critical | RCE, auth bypass completo, compromissione massiva di dati | €2.000–€5.000+ |
| High | Privilege escalation, IDOR con dati sensibili, SSRF significativo | €750–€2.000 |
| Medium | XSS significativo, CSRF con impatto, access-control flaw limitato | €250–€750 |
| Low | Information disclosure limitata, hardening issue con impatto concreto | €50–€250 |

La bounty finale viene determinata caso per caso in base a exploitability, impatto, scope, qualità del report e presenza di duplicati.

## Regole di responsible disclosure
1. Testare esclusivamente sistemi e funzionalità autorizzati.
2. Fermarsi dopo aver dimostrato l'impatto minimo necessario.
3. Non esfiltrare, modificare o cancellare dati non necessari.
4. Non rendere pubblica la vulnerabilità prima della risoluzione o di un accordo esplicito.
5. Includere nel report: asset interessato, prerequisiti, passi di riproduzione, evidenza, impatto e remediation suggerita.
6. Per vulnerabilità critiche, contattare il team security con priorità.

## Triage
- Conferma ricezione: target < 2 business days
- Triage iniziale: target < 5 business days
- Valutazione severità: CVSS + business impact
- Duplicati: bounty al primo report riproducibile e sufficientemente dettagliato
- Pagamento: dopo validazione e classificazione della vulnerabilità

## Metasploit
Metasploit può essere utilizzato come supporto alla validazione **solo su target autorizzati**. Non è consentito lanciare moduli distruttivi, persistence, credential theft o payload contro sistemi di terzi.

## Disclosure
Il programma è orientato alla responsible disclosure. Eventuali disclosure coordinate saranno concordate con il team MyZubster caso per caso.

> **Nota:** questa issue definisce la proposta operativa del bounty program. Prima dell'apertura pubblica è necessario confermare contatti security, metodo di pagamento, termini legali e asset definitivi in scope.

- Verify communication between the Open-FDD services.
- Confirm that the web application is accessible through a Railway-generated HTTPS URL.

- Test service restarts and redeployment using updated GHCR images.

### 2. Application security review

Perform an authorized security review of the Open-FDD application deployed specifically for testing.

Review areas should include:

- Authentication and authorization

- Exposed API endpoints
- JWT handling
- Cross-site scripting and injection vulnerabilities
- Improperly exposed environment variables or secrets
- Container and network exposure
- MQTT authentication and topic authorization
- TLS/HTTPS configuration
- Rate limiting and input validation
- Dependency and container-image vulnerabilities

A small pilot bounty may be offered for valid, reproducible, previously unreported vulnerabilities. Proposed reward: $25 per accepted vulnerability, subject to the published scope, exclusions, verification requirements, and an overall program budget.

`BACnet environment → edge gateway → MQTT over TLS → Railway → Open-FDD`

Validate:

- BACnet data collection
- Conversion into the expected MQTT payload format
- MQTT authentication
- Encrypted MQTTS communication
- Topic naming and permissions
- Reconnection after network interruptions
- Duplicate and out-of-order messages

- Data ingestion by Open-FDD
- Visibility of received data in the historian, API, and UI
- Logging without exposing credentials or sensitive data

Testing is limited to the designated Open-FDD Railway test deployment.

The following are prohibited:

- Testing Railway infrastructure or other Railway customers
- Denial-of-service or load testing without prior approval
- Destructive testing or intentional data loss
- Social engineering or phishing

Stop testing and report the issue immediately if sensitive information, credentials, or access to an unrelated system is discovered.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

### Additional Team Members

I am requesting this bounty as an individual, however my work was made possible thanks to Shielded Labs funding my LLM-assisted auditing research as well as the audit that found this bug. ZODL's and Zcash Foundation's teams and leadership deserve an immense amount of credit for patching the vulnerability in an unprecedented security response (really the best I have ever seen in my career!).
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

I was around when the program grew out of discussions here on the forums!

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$750,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting a bug bounty for responsibly disclosing the Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability, which likely prevented the loss of $2.3B USD worth of ZEC. Funding this bounty supports Zcash's long-term security: it sends a message to security researchers that they can report potentially-devastating counterfeiting vulnerabilities and have a good chance of getting paid legitimately, reducing the incentive to exploit counterfeiting vulnerabilities maliciously.

### Project Description

I am applying for a bug bounty as a result of finding and responsibly disclosing the recent Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability. I found the bug while developing AI-assisted security auditing tools and performing Zcash security audits as a contractor for Shielded Labs, though I am applying for the grant as an individual.

If the vulnerability had been exploited, it would have allowed an unlimited amount of ZEC to be minted within the Orchard pool. If an attacker exploited the bug, they could have effectively "stolen" all of the funds in the Orchard pool. At the time, Orchard contained around 4.2M ZEC, worth $2.3B USD. Without my timely disclosure, the bug could have been found and exploited by a malicious actor using AI tools.

Funding this bounty is important for Zcash's long-term security. It sends a message to security researchers: if you find a catastrophic counterfeiting bug in Zcash, you can report it honestly, request a bounty through a retroactive grant (even though there isn't a formal bug bounty program), and have a good chance of getting paid legitimately.

*Funding this bounty reduces the incentive to attack Zcash.* This is especially important as a fallback in the absence of a formal bug bounty program; ZCG's bounty program was [closed](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/closing-the-zcg-vulnerability-bounty-program/55855) just days before I discovered the bug! Hopefully this was the last counterfeiting vulnerability Zcash will ever have, but just in case it isn't, this precedent will help encourage future bug-discoverers to do the right thing.

Asking for $750,000 is a lot, so it's important to justify that number. The bounty programs of several major projects suggest an award of [10% of the affected funds](https://immunefi.com/blog/industry-trends/a-defi-security-standard-the-scaling-bug-bounty/) up to maximums of around $1M-$2M (e.g. [1](https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/compoundfinance/information/), [2](https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/optimism/information/)):

> "Critical bug bounty payouts should be priced as a percentage of the economic damage they would have caused, so that even blackhats are incentivized to review code and disclose vulnerabilities, thereby reducing malicious exploits. For most DeFi projects, that’s 10% of TVL at risk." — Immunefi

I'd rather keep my ask below industry norms, and I've already received some gifts, so I am asking for an amount that's reasonable in proportion to the harms that were prevented, and which will help me continue to expand the ways I can contribute to Zcash. The following table will help you compare my ask to a sampling of similar cases:

| Precedent | Vulnerability / impact | Funds at risk (approx.) | Bounty | Ratio (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Wormhole, 2022 — satya0x](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/wormhole-uninitialized-proxy-bugfix-review/) | Uninitialized implementation contract allowed an attacker-controlled Guardian set and SELFDESTRUCT of the implementation, bricking the Ethereum bridge and locking its assets | $1.8B in the contract at time of submission | $10,000,000 | 0.56% |
| [Aurora, 2022 — pwning.eth](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/aurora-inflation-spend-bugfix-review-6m-payout/) | "Infinite spend" allowing repeated balance doubling; effectively infinite ETH creation in the Aurora Engine | 70,000 ETH ($204M) plus $200M in other assets | $6,000,000 | 1.48% |
| [Optimism, 2022 — Jay Freeman (saurik)](https://medium.com/immunefi/optimism-infinite-money-duplication-bugfix-review-daa6597146a0) | Unlimited creation of OETH; counterfeit OETH could drain DEXes and bridged assets | $322.5M TVL | $2,000,042 | 0.62% |
| [Polygon, 2021 — Gerhard Wagner](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/polygon-double-spend-bugfix-review-2m-bounty/) | Plasma Bridge replay/double-spend allowing one burn transaction to be exited up to 223 times | $850M | $2,000,000 | 0.24% |
| [Belt Finance, 2021 — Alexander Schlindwein](https://medium.com/immunefi/belt-finance-logic-error-bug-fix-postmortem-39308a158291) | Logic error produced excess shares; repeatable until the contract was drained | $60M (single iteration $10M) | $1,050,000 total ($1M Belt + $50k BSC match) | 1.75% |
| **My request**| **Unlimited, undetectable creation of counterfeit ZEC within Orchard** | **$2.29B (4.2M ZEC at $545)** | **$750,000** | **0.033%** |

Comparing funds-at-risk to bounty reward ratios, the reward ratio I am asking for is 1/7th of the smallest ratio in the table above.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

In September of 2025, I started developing tools for security auditing using LLMs. My intention was to automate as much of my manual security audit process as possible. The models that existed at the time weren't that smart, so this took a lot of prompt engineering, but it worked.

I continued developing the tools throughout 2026 and started running them against Zcash-adjacent software like the Keystone hardware wallet and found some bugs. I've open-sourced this general-purpose AI auditing framework on GitHub: [defuse/auditician](https://github.com/defuse/auditician) (this is not a deliverable for this grant).

Later on, Shielded Labs hired me as a contractor to continue this work and audit more Zcash-related software. I ended up developing a new set of agents specifically for auditing Zcash. Using those agents to audit Orchard's balance integrity properties, with Opus 4.8 the day after it was released, was what ultimately found this bug.

In brief, the agent framework that found the bug is based on the principle that a bug becomes transparent to an LLM when it has everything it needs to spot the bug right there in its context window: the security property that's violated, good ideas for how that security property can be attacked, and all of the relevant code and specification text. To make that happen, the tool:

1. First helps you clearly define the security property you're trying to attack (in this case, Orchard balance integrity).
2. Then it enumerates all relevant statements in the protocol specification and ZIPs, all relevant security sub-properties, all possible failure modes (attack ideas), and all relevant code locations. This requires running several rounds of expansion to find everything.
3. Then it passes small batches of the enumerated items to agents designed for specific auditing purposes: A design-auditor checks if the specification itself contains any vulnerabilities, a failure-mode-auditor checks if any of the attack ideas actually work, a code-auditor spends time looking for vulnerabilities in a region of code, and a security-property-auditor exhaustively checks whether a claimed security property is true or false.
4. Finally, an issue validator agent then validates and tries to expand on all of the security issues that come out of this process.

The day after Opus 4.8 was released, I set this framework running to audit Orchard's balance integrity. A few hours later it found the vulnerability, which had been missed by all of my prior AI-assisted (and manual) audits of Orchard.

At first I couldn't believe the bug was real, but Claude's explanation sounded correct. I used Claude to help me develop a series of proof of concepts, starting by writing a small circuit that just used the vulnerable component, which proved to me that a critical circuit constraint was actually missing. 

I immediately reported the issue to ZODL, then, working overnight, I had Claude develop a full proof of concept as an RPC test within `zcashd`. The RPC test proved the issue was exploitable by creating millions of "regtest" ZEC on my local node (regtest is `zcashd`'s testing mode, none of this ever hit a live chain). Having the ability to create infinite ZEC right in front of me was honestly the craziest emotional experience of my life; while I'd like to think that I'd do the right thing in any case, my shared history with and love for the Zcash engineers, who pretty much raised me intellectually and morally, and the possibility of applying for this grant, made it a lot easier to make the right choice.

I spent the next weeks helping the ZODL and ZF engineers by reviewing and testing the patches that temporarily disabled the Orchard pool to close off the vulnerability, as well as the changes that eventually re-enabled a secure Orchard pool.

The full details can be found in [Shielded Labs' blog post](https://shieldedlabs.net/the-orchard-counterfeiting-vulnerability/) and my [work log](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SVK41y-ip3Vw9eB69E9QRy-Qn3idTOwV/view).

### Time Period of Work Completion

May 2026 - June 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

The bug was discovered at little financial cost (aside from self-funding my own research prior to being hired by Shielded Labs) thanks to judicious use of Claude's Max plan. The amount requested is based on the harm to ZEC holders that was prevented and to set a reasonable precedent that makes Zcash safer, not a reimbursement for expenses.

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

I have not received any prior funding from the Zcash Coinholder Grants Program. In 2022-2023, I received funding from ZCG for my [Zcash Ecosystem Security Lead](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcash-ecosystem-security-lead/42090) grant.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

I received one substantial gift as well as some smaller ones in response to [this tweet](https://x.com/DefuseSec/status/2062927120775750029?s=20). Shielded Labs paid me at my regular consulting rate for the Zcash-specific research and auditing work. I have chosen to request an amount below the industry norms cited above.

### Success Metrics

Assuming the bug was not exploited during the four-year period of vulnerability (it looks like it wasn't), this work prevented unbounded inflation within the Orchard pool, possibly resulting in the loss of all Orchard ZEC. This would have been devastating not only to everyone who held Orchard ZEC but also to Zcash's reputation as a safe, private store of value.

The discovery of this bug also led the community to develop and deploy the formally-verified Ironwood pool, which aims to mathematically close off the possibility of similar bugs being found in that pool as well as the current Orchard pool. (I did not contribute to Ironwood's development, aside from some security review.)

### Proof of completion

A full writeup, as well as my work log, is available in [Shielded Labs' blog post](https://shieldedlabs.net/the-orchard-counterfeiting-vulnerability/). 

See also [ZODL's post](https://zodl.com/orchard-vulnerability-successfully-remediated/) and [Zcash Foundation's post](https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/) about the vulnerability.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

I'm a board member of the Zcash Foundation, I am an independent contractor doing work for Shielded Labs, and I own various stocks and cryptocurrencies, including ZEC. The Zcash Foundation is one of the keyholders for the disbursement of funds from this grant program, as is Shielded Labs, so I will recuse myself from any discussion around supporting/vetoing/funding grants in this round, as well as anything else related to coinholder grants voting. I will not vote for my proposal with my own coins. I've reviewed ZIP-1016 and I believe I am eligible to apply for this grant as an individual.

## Coverage gap report (NOT a confirmed bug — needs verification)

**Verdict:** UNFILED surface. No reproduction performed in this report; this documents a verb the bounty's agent harness cannot observe and that has **0** filed issues.

### Evidence the surface is uncovered
1. The canonical monk-agent MCP tool inventory (`plugins/monk/skills/monk/SKILL.md`, `allowed-tools`, line 4 of current `monk-plugin` HEAD) lists **every** exposed agent tool. cluster tools expose status/peers/create/grow/peer-*/upgrade/delete/exit/provider/price/catalog/gpuTypes/estimate/ingress-*/registry-*/forget/switch/join/bind — there is **no** `monk_cluster_inspect` tool.
2. Live issue search (`repo:monk-io/monk-plugin is:issue "cluster inspect"`) returns **13** match(es) — only [342, 327, 245, 250, 243] (different verb).
3. `monk cluster inspect` exists in the monk CLI per the docs / other issues, so it is a live, shippable verb with no agent coverage and no bug reports.

### Why this is a false-success risk (to verify)  [DUP-RISK live hits [342, 327, 245, 250, 243]]
`cluster inspect` returns cluster state. Sibling status verbs misreport on RPC failure (#244 peers RPC fail, #250 status-read fail, #298 ingress.status disabled-on-RPC-fail). `inspect` may return cached/stale/partial cluster state while reporting ok, leaving the agent blind to a degraded cluster.

### Evidence bar to reach +2 (for whoever can run a live monkd)
- **R (reachability):** run `monk cluster inspect`, then prove the dependent endpoint is actually live — `curl -v <endpoint>` returning 200 / valid TLS, **or** capture the failure monk reported as success.
- **S (secret-injection):** run with a test secret, confirm via `monk secret list` / runtime env that the secret is present at runtime; show the "success" report when injection actually failed.

### Status
- Filed as: coverage gap / **needs-verification** (Gate HOLD_NO_REPRO — no execution in this report).
- If a concrete false-success is reproduced, link it here; this issue is the tracking anchor.

title: 🔒 Smart Contract Security Audit Request
body:
## Objective
Conduct a comprehensive security audit of these TON smart contracts to identify vulnerabilities within the scope of the [TON Bug Bounty Program](https://github.com/ton-blockchain/bug-bounty).

Be sure to read this before completing the assignment https://github.com/ton-blockchain/bug-bounty/blob/main/skills/bug-bounty-self-check.md

## Scope (In-Scope Vulnerabilities)

### Critical & High Severity
- **Fund Theft**: Any vulnerability allowing unauthorized transfer of funds
- **Signature Bypass**: Bypassing signature verification
- **Replay Attacks**: Replaying transactions without proper protection
- **Sequence Number Bypass**: Bypassing seqno checks
- **Integer Overflow/Underflow**: Arithmetic errors leading to fund loss
- **Logic Errors**: Flaws in contract logic allowing unauthorized actions
- **Gas Manipulation**: Forcing contract to run out of gas at critical moments
- **Message Spoofing**: Forging messages from trusted sources

### Medium Severity
- **Denial of Service**: Making contract permanently unusable
- **Information Leakage**: Exposing sensitive information via contract state
- **Upgrade Vulnerabilities**: Flaws in upgrade mechanisms
- **Access Control Issues**: Improper permission checks

### Low Severity
- **Gas Inefficiency**: Suboptimal gas usage (only if it creates attack vectors)
- **Code Quality Issues**: Only if they have security implications

## Out of Scope
- UI/UX issues
- Missing features without security impact
- Gas optimization without security impact
- Known TON blockchain limitations

## Smart Contract Attack Vectors to Check

### 1. Message Handling
- [ ] Verify all incoming messages are properly validated
- [ ] Check `op` (operation code) handling
- [ ] Verify sender authentication
- [ ] Check for message replay protection (seqno, valid_until)
- [ ] Verify proper handling of bounced messages

### 2. Signature Verification
- [ ] Verify signature is checked for all privileged operations
- [ ] Check for signature malleability issues
- [ ] Verify public key is properly stored and used
- [ ] Check for missing signature checks

### 3. State Management
- [ ] Verify state is properly initialized
- [ ] Check for race conditions in state updates
- [ ] Verify state consistency after operations
- [ ] Check for improper state exposure

### 4. Fund Management
- [ ] Verify balance checks before transfers
- [ ] Check for integer overflow in amount calculations
- [ ] Verify proper handling of TON vs Jetton
- [ ] Check for dust attacks vulnerability

### 5. TVM-Specific Issues
- [ ] Check for gas consumption issues
- [ ] Verify proper use of TVM primitives
- [ ] Check for cell/slice handling errors
- [ ] Verify proper exception handling

### 6. Wallet-Specific (for wallet-contract)
- [ ] Verify seqno increment logic
- [ ] Check valid_until implementation
- [ ] Verify multi-signature logic (if applicable)
- [ ] Check for sub-wallet ID vulnerabilities

### 7. Multisig-Specific (for multisig-contract)
- [ ] Verify signature collection logic
- [ ] Check for signature replay across different proposals
- [ ] Verify quorum enforcement
- [ ] Check for proposer authorization

### 8. Token-Specific (for token-contract)
- [ ] Verify mint/burn authorization
- [ ] Check for balance manipulation
- [ ] Verify transfer logic
- [ ] Check for approval/allowance vulnerabilities

### 9. DNS-Specific (for dns-contract)
- [ ] Verify domain ownership checks
- [ ] Check for DNS record manipulation
- [ ] Verify proper resolution logic

### 10. Nominator Pool-Specific (for nominator-pool)
- [ ] Verify stake/unstake logic
- [ ] Check for reward calculation errors
- [ ] Verify validator authorization
- [ ] Check for fund locking issues

## Methodology

### Phase 1: Code Comprehension
1. Read entire contract code
2. Map all functions and their purposes
3. Identify entry points (recv_internal, recv_external)
4. Map state variables and their purposes
5. Understand the contract's role in TON ecosystem

### Phase 2: Threat Modeling
1. Identify trusted parties (owner, validator, etc.)
2. Identify untrusted parties (anyone sending messages)
3. Map trust boundaries
4. Identify critical assets (funds, state)
5. List potential attackers and their goals

### Phase 3: Vulnerability Analysis
For each function:
1. Check input validation
2. Verify authorization checks
3. Analyze state changes
4. Check for integer overflow/underflow
5. Verify proper error handling
6. Check for gas-related issues

### Phase 4: Attack Simulation
For each potential vulnerability:
1. Construct attack scenario
2. Write PoC in Fift or use TON Sandbox
3. Verify exploit works
4. Assess impact

## Deliverables

For EACH vulnerability found, create a separate issue with:

### Issue Title Format
`[Security] <Severity>: <Brief Description> in <Contract Name>`

Example: `[Security] Critical: Signature Bypass in Wallet V4 seqno check`

### Issue Template
```markdown
## Vulnerability Details

**Severity**: Critical / High / Medium / Low
**CVSS Score**: [0.0-10.0]
**CVSS Vector**: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H]
**Vulnerability Type**: [CWE ID and Name]
**Affected Contract**: [Contract name and file path]
**Affected Function**: [Function name]
**Affected Lines**: [Line numbers]

## Description
[Detailed technical description of the vulnerability]

## Root Cause
[Why this vulnerability exists - the underlying flaw]

## Impact
[What an attacker can achieve]
- Financial impact: [How much can be stolen/lost]
- Operational impact: [What functionality is compromised]

## Proof of Concept (PoC)

### Attack Scenario
[Step-by-step description of the attack]

### PoC Code (Fift/Python)
```fift
// Fift code demonstrating the exploit
```

OR

```python
# Python code using pytonlib or TON Sandbox
```

### Expected Behavior
[What should happen according to contract logic]

### Actual Behavior
[What actually happens - the exploit]

### Transaction Trace
[If available, show the transaction flow]

## Remediation

### Root Cause Fix
[How to fix the underlying issue]

### Code Fix
```func
// Before (vulnerable)
() vulnerable_function(...) inline {
    // vulnerable code
}

// After (fixed)
() fixed_function(...) inline {
    // fixed code
}
```

### Additional Recommendations
[Any additional security improvements]

## References
- [Link to CWE]
- [Link to similar vulnerability in other projects]
- [Link to TON documentation]
- [Link to TON Bug Bounty scope]

## Self-Check Validation
- [ ] Verified this is in-scope for TON Bug Bounty
- [ ] Confirmed this is not a known/documented issue
- [ ] PoC tested in isolated environment (TON Sandbox, NOT mainnet/testnet)
- [ ] Impact assessment is accurate and realistic
- [ ] Remediation is practical and doesn't break functionality
- [ ] No false positives - vulnerability is real and exploitable

## Execution Instructions

1. **Read all contracts thoroughly**: Don't skip any file
2. **Understand the ecosystem**: How do these contracts interact?
3. **Think like an attacker**: What would YOU try to exploit?
4. **Verify everything**: Double-check each finding
5. **Create separate issues**: One issue per vulnerability
6. **Prioritize by severity**: Critical first, then High, Medium, Low
7. **Tag appropriately**: Use labels like `security`, `critical`, `smart-contract`, `wallet`, `multisig`, etc.
8. **No false positives**: Only report what you can prove with PoC

## Special Considerations

### For Wallet Contracts
- Focus on seqno, valid_until, signature verification
- Check for replay attack vectors
- Verify sub-wallet ID handling

### For Multisig Contracts
- Focus on signature collection and verification
- Check for quorum enforcement
- Verify proposal lifecycle

### For Token Contracts
- Focus on mint/burn authorization
- Check for balance manipulation
- Verify transfer and approval logic

### For DNS Contracts
- Focus on domain ownership verification
- Check for record manipulation

### For Nominator Pools
- Focus on stake/unstake logic
- Check for reward calculation
- Verify validator interactions

## Context Management
You have unlimited time and context. The context autocompacts, so you can continue indefinitely. Do as much as possible in one go. If something is left over, continue in the same issue until fully complete.

## Repository to Audit
https://github.com/xlabtg/wallet-contract

**CRITICAL WARNING**: 
- Do NOT deploy or test exploits on mainnet or testnet
- Use TON Sandbox or local test environment only
- This is for security research purposes only
- Follow responsible disclosure practices

title: Harden VCS runner against GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT override
body:
`packages/vcs/runner.go` documents that autonomous VCS operations must never block on terminal credential prompts, but `mergeEnv()` currently sets `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` **before** applying caller overrides. A caller can therefore pass `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=1` and re-enable blocking prompts. Proposed fix: - apply caller environment overrides first - force `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` last (or explicitly reject attempts to override it) - extend `TestMergeEnvDisablesTerminalPrompts` with an override map containing `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=1` and assert the merged environment still contains `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` Do not edit this symbol until the repository-required GitNexus checks can be run. `AGENTS.md` requires `impact({target: "mergeEnv", direction: "upstream"})` before editing and `detect_changes({scope: "compare", base_ref: "main"})` before committing. GitNexus is not currently available in the connected toolset.
